This question illustrates the aggregation principle. Maurice may aggregate his claims against O’Connell, even though they arise out of separate transactions, because they are asserted against only one party. So A is wrong; Maurice meets the amount requirement against O’Connell. But he cannot aggregate his claims against O’Connor with those against Parker, so B is wrong too. C suggests that Maurice could aggregate his claims against these two defendants if they arose from the same underlying transaction. That isn’t true under the general rule, which requires separate satisfaction of the amount requirement against each defendant, regardless of how closely their claims are connected. D takes the cake. Maurice clearly satisfies the amount requirement against O’Connor, so this choice is doubly wrong. Here’s another variation on the theme:

Final answer: A

This question tests your understanding of how the amount-incontroversy requirement works when there are multiple parties involved. A fails, because under pre§1367 case law, each plaintiff must independently meet the amount requirement. Here, Moe doesn’t seek enough to meet it. B also fails; Curly’s counterclaim will not support subject matter jurisdiction over the case. Only Larry’s claim supports jurisdiction here, so we look only to that to determine whether the amount requirement is satisfied. And it isn’t, since Larry seeks less than $75,001. C passes muster. Even though Larry sues two defendants, he may recover the full $100,001 from either, depending upon who the jury finds responsible for the collision. D fails too. Although Larry seeks more than $75,010 overall, he cannot aggregate these claims against separate defendants to meet the amount requirement. Final answer: C

This question illustrates how difficult it can be to determine someone’s domicile. Let’s look at B first. This choice suggests that Filbert is still domiciled in Illinois, because he didn’t intend to remain indefinitely in Nebraska when he went there. But this isn’t right. When he left Illinois, he intended to return within three years. However, once he got into his second year, he changed his mind about returning to Illinois. At that point, he had no intention of going back to Illinois, and planned instead to live in Nebraska permanently. So, during his second year, he became domiciled in Nebraska. His change of heart about staying in Nebraska meant that the two requirements for acquiring a domicile coincided in Nebraska. He lived there, and intended to remain there indefinitely. Once those two things came true simultaneously, he lost his Illinois domicile and gained a Nebraska domicile. Now, what about C? This choice argues that Filbert is domiciled in Colorado. Why? Well, he was working in Colorado over the summer, and then decided to accept their offer of permanent employment. Doesn’t that mean that he formed the intent to remain in Colorado indefinitely? Nope. To form a domicile in a place, you’ve got to both reside there and intend to remain there indefinitely. While Filbert was in Colorado, he didn’t intend to remain there indefinitely. He thought he’d be leaving after the summer. Only later, when he was already back in Nebraska, did he decide to go to Colorado. But he wasn’t in Colorado any longer! He couldn’t acquire a Colorado domicile based solely on his decision to go there sometime in the future. That wouldn’t satisfy the residency requirement. How about D? This choice asserts that Filbert is domiciled in Nebraska because he currently resides there and does not intend to return to Illinois. But remember, domicile requires more than just current residence plus lack of intent to return to some other state. It also requires the intent to remain in the present state indefinitely. Here, Filbert clearly does not intend to remain in Nebraska indefinitely. He intends to leave upon graduating from law school. Thus, he fails the intent-to-remain-inde-finitely part of the test. So, A takes the prize. Although Filbert is currently living in Nebraska, he does not intend to remain there indefinitely. And although he intends to remain in Colorado indefinitely, he does not presently reside there. Therefore, the last state in which these two elements coincided was Nebraska. There, Filbert resided and intended to remain indefinitely. Until he establishes a new domicile elsewhere, he retains his Nebraska domicile.

Final answer: A

This question illustrates two important points about federal subject matter jurisdiction. First, the party who files suit may change positions regarding the existence of jurisdiction during the course of litigation. Here, Taney initially filed suit based upon a theory of federal jurisdiction, but then changed his mind after the case had proceeded for several months. Second, the court can raise the issue of subject matter jurisdiction sua sponte—on its own initiative—and dismiss the case if it finds that it lacks authority to hear it. C suggests that Taney waives all challenges to subject matter jurisdiction simply by filing suit in federal court. This isn’t so; a plaintiff may challenge the court’s jurisdiction at any time before judgment is entered. D takes this one step further, suggesting that Taney waived his right to object to the court’s jurisdiction by proceeding with the case for ten months without asserting such an objection. But again, this is not true. A party may assert an objection to subject matter jurisdiction at any point prior to entry of judgment. So both C and D fail. That leaves us with B and A. Both suggest that the court would grant the motion if the case did not meet constitutional requirements for a proper ‘‘case or controversy.’’ However, A argues that the court could properly deny the motion if the case met constitutional standards, even though it didn’t meet statutory standards. Not so! If the statute doesn’t authorize the court to hear the case, it shouldn’t. It makes little sense to allow the court to hear cases that Congress hasn’t authorized it to hear, just because the Constitution allows them. So B is the best choice here.

Final answer: B

This question illustrates how the broad reading of arising-under jurisdiction in Article Ill, §2 leads to a very different result from the narrow reading of that term in Section 1331. D is the best choice here. The Mottleys’ case arises out of a dispute about a state contract, so it cannot be removed to federal court under Section 1331, as construed in Mottley. But the state court’s judgment rests upon two rulings concerning federal law: first, that the federal statute bars renewal of the Mottley’s passes, and second, that the statute violates the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment. Both of those rulings constitute interpretations of ‘‘the . . . laws of the United States,’’ within the meaning of Article III, §2. So the case arises under federal law, within the meaning of the constitutional grant of jurisdiction. Therefore, the Supreme Court has the constitutional authority to review the state court’s decision. And, under Section 1257(a), it also has the statutory authority to review the case. That section authorizes review whenever the state court’s decision rests on a ruling that a federal statute is unconstitutional, or that a state statute conflicts with federal law. Here, the state court ruled that the federal statute was unconstitutional, and that it barred renewal of the Mottleys‘ passes. So the Supreme Court clearly has the authority to review the case. C suggests that Section 1257 is unconstitutionally overbroad, because it authorizes review of cases that arise under state law. But there’s nothing wrong with that! The statute simply gives the Supreme Court discretionary authority to review certain types of decisions by state courts, whether they arise under state or federal law. Nothing in the Constitution prevents Congress from giving the Supreme Court such authority. B takes the position that the Court couldn’t review the state court’s construction of the federal statute, because that isn’t a ‘‘federal question’’ within the meaning of Section 1257. But surely it is. The statute says that the Court may review state court decisions that construe federal statutes, as well as those that invalidate them. And A is just plain silly. The Mottleys’ suit arises under state contract law, true enough. But it also arises under federal law, because the state court based its decision on a federal statute and a provision of the Federal Constitution. So the case arises under federal as well as state law. I suppose you’re wondering what happened to poor little E. Well, the Mottleys really existed, and their names really were Erasmus and Annie. See Mottley v. Louisiana, 69 F. Supp. 607 (S.D.N.Y.) aff’d sub nom., Louisiana ex rel. Francis v. Resweber, 329 U.S. 459 (1946). Now let’s look at another situation in which a party wants to litigate a federal issue in federal court, but the other side objects that the case doesn’t properly belong there. In the next chapter we’ll examine the removal statute, which allows a defendant who is sued in state court to transfer the action to federal court. Before leaving the subject of arising-under jurisdiction, however, take a moment to work through this problem, which tests your understanding of the difference between the constitutional standard and the statutory standard for arising-under jurisdiction.

Final answer: D

This one isn’t hard once you parse the choices carefully. A is wrong; even though the amount-incontroversy requirement hasn’t been satisfied here, the objection comes too late. It is based on a jurisdictional defect—lack of subject matter jurisdiction—but it still must be raised within thirty days of removal, unless it goes to the very power of the federal court to hear the case at all—that is, its subject matter jurisdiction. Here, the federal court clearly has subject matter jurisdiction over the case, so the objection may not be asserted more than thirty days after removal. B fails as well. True enough, Ivens didn’t join in the removal, but that doesn’t mean that the case couldn’t be removed. It means that the case can—and probably will—be sent back down to state court. D also misses the point. Even assuming that the case is within the federal diversity statute, it won’t be heard in federal court, because Ivens objects to removal. Since he didn’t join in the removal, the case will go back to state court. So what about C? It takes the prize. The court has original jurisdiction over the case, since it arises under federal law. However, Ivens’s objection to removal has been waived, because it is not based on lack of subject matter jurisdiction, yet was filed more than thirty days after removal. Thus, the case will proceed in federal court. Note how important it is to read these questions closely. In this case, the key fact is that the action arose under federal law. That makes the case removable, but it also means that the court has authority to hear it. Once we realize that, we see that C is right, because the objection to removal is untimely.

Final answer: C

This question illustrates several important points about removal. First, it shows how the timing of events affects removability. When Rasmussen filed suit, he had only a state law claim against Apex. Since there was no independent ground for federal subject matter jurisdiction over the case, it wasn’t removable. But once he added the federal age discrimination claim, the case became removable. It now included two claims, one within the federal court’s jurisdiction and another within its supplemental jurisdiction. Under §1367(a), the federal court has authority to hear the entire case, including the state law claim, since they arise out of the same case or controversy. And since the amended case includes a claim within the federal court’s jurisdiction, it becomes removable under §1441(a). D takes the position that the state law claim isn’t removable, even though the federal claim is. That’s wrong. Once the federal claim is added, the case as a whole is removable, because it contains a claim within the federal court’s original jurisdiction and others within its supplemental jurisdiction. B suggests that the presence of an in-state party prevents removal. Not quite right. There is an in-state party here—Rasmussen—but he is a plaintiff, not a defendant. Section 1441(b)(2)’s limitation applies only where there is an in-state defendant. C also fails. True, Rasmussen might have removed the case based on diversity, since he is diverse from Apex. However, he didn’t do so. Instead, he chose to file in state court. His failure to remove does not bar Apex from removing later, once the case becomes removable. So A wins. Note that the fact that three months passed before the amendment doesn’t prevent removal. Removal is proper whenever the case becomes removable, unless the time limits for removal have expired. We’ll discuss those next.

Final answer: A

This question illustrates how courts balance the interests of the parties in determining whether they should exercise jurisdiction over a defendant from another state. Here, D is right; C is wrong. It may seem unfair to require Mary to return to California to litigate the case, since she went there as a visitor and did not seek out relations with California. However, the Supreme Court has held that, if a person travels into a state (even briefly) and causes an accident while driving on public roads, he or she has established sufficient ties to the forum to support specific in personam jurisdiction based on those activities. Burnham v. Superior Court, 495 U.S. 604 (1990). This rule makes sense, because people who drive on public highways enter the ‘‘stream of commerce’’ in the forum state and expose themselves to liability arising from their actions there. A is also wrong here. Even though Mary entered California solely to visit her daughter, she still engaged in purposeful activity there by renting a car and driving on public streets. B fails too. Although it might be very burdensome for Mary to return to California to defend the lawsuit, due process analysis focuses primarily on the burden imposed on the plaintiff, rather than the defendant. If the defendant’s conduct supports jurisdiction under International Shoe, the fact that defending the case in the chosen forum will impose some hardship on the defendant generally won’t prevent the court from exercising jurisdiction. In most cases, the plaintiff chose the forum because it was convenient for him or her, so it seems fairer to make the defendant bear any resulting inconvenience. But see World-Wide Volkswagen Corp. v. Woodson, 444 U.S. 286, 304 n.17 (1980), suggesting that the convenience of the parties is a factor in assessing reasonableness. So, although the Due Process Clause allows the California court to hear this case against Mary, it probably wouldn’t allow it to assert jurisdiction over her if she came to California just to vacation at Disneyland and got into an auto accident during her stay. That kind of contact—being present temporarily for purely personal reasons—is insufficient to establish minimum contacts. See Asahi Metal Industry Co., Ltd. v. Superior Court, 480 U.S. 102, 112 (1987).

Final answer: D

This one is tricky. A suggests that Dispos-All should only be subject to specific in personam jurisdiction if it engaged in some affirmative conduct directed at Maryland—advertising, establishing a distribution system, etc.—as World-Wide Volkswagen did. But this is a different kind of case; here, the defendant’s activities were confined to another state but had effects in Maryland. So A misses the point. B also fails, because Dispos-All didn’t reach out to Maryland, yet still caused injury there through its operations in Delaware. C captures the essence of the analysis. If you deliberately engage in activity that creates risks outside your home state, you will likely be held amenable to suit where those risks materialize. See Calder v. Jones, 465 U.S. 783 (1984). D is wrong, because the ‘‘stream of commerce’’ concept doesn’t apply here. That doctrine applies when goods are sent into the forum state, either directly or indirectly via distributors. Here, the waste was dumped in Delaware, though it could migrate to Maryland. And, while the migration might be foreseeable, it wasn’t intended. So C wins.

Final answer: C

In A, Ohora seeks to sue Roux for damages caused by his negligence in maintaining the premises where she fell. There is nothing about Roux himself within the state; he does’t live there, work there, own anything there, or do anything else there. However, Ohora has attached the land on which she fell, and asks the court to dispose of Roux’s interest in that land if it finds that he was negligent. Since the land is located in Nebraska, the court can clearly exert authority over it. And since Roux owns the land, the court can certainly decide whether he should keep it or lose it. Thus, the court will have power to enter judgment for Ohora, and to enforce that judgment by ordering sale of the land to satisfy the judgment. Under the old analysis, this would be proper quasi in rem jurisdiction, very type II. After Shaffer, however, it seems doubtful that this would still be allowed. Shaffer suggests that the court cannot seize Roux’s real estate unless it could otherwise assert jurisdiction over Roux directly for the tort claim. That would require some contact by Roux with Nebraska related to the claim. His ownership of the land may well suffice, since the accident occurred on the land. See Burnham v. Superior Court, 495 U.S. 604, 610 n.1 (1990); see generally Wright & Miller, Federal Practice and Procedure §1067.2. B involves a suit to determine rights in specific property, here Ohora’s farm. This is a true in rem case, involving direct disposition of the res—the farm—in light of competing claims to it. Such suits were never challenged before Shaffer, and they remain valid after Shaffer. C is another quasi in rem case, very type I. Here, the court’s authority over the crane allows it to resolve the parties’ dispute concerning their respective interests in it. Again, this was always considered proper, even though the parties’ dispute doesn’t arise out of the presence of the crane in Nebraska. And again, it remains proper after Shaffer. The Court made it quite clear that it wasn’t rejecting all exercises of quasi in rem jurisdiction, just those like Heitner’s, which amounted to an indirect method of bringing the defendant into court. So D is the best choice. Let me give you two more examples illustrating the limits of post-Shaffer attachment jurisdiction.

Final answer: D

Shaffer does not hold that either type I or type III quasi in rem jurisdiction is unconstitutional. Indeed, the case doesn’t even mention those two forms of quasi in rem jurisdiction. Nor does it suggest that they should be analyzed differently than before. Thus A is wrong; it suggests that Shaffer holds that all three types of in rem jurisdiction are unconstitutional. B also fails, since Shaffer does not reject both type I and type II quasi in rem jurisdiction. It rejects only type II. C takes the prize. Shaffer rejected the use of quasi in rem type II jurisdiction, but left open the possibility that quasi in rem type I jurisdiction might still be constitutionally exercised. After Shaffer, if you want to sue someone on an unrelated claim, you can’t do it just because you have attached some of their property within your borders. You will need to establish personal jurisdiction over the defendant herself, using minimum contacts analysis. However, if you seek to recover specific property located in the forum, you may still do so through quasi in rem type I jurisdiction. Let me give you one more example involving the reach of Shaffer.

Final answer: C

This question illustrates how the choice of court affects the standard for determining whether there is personal jurisdiction over a defendant. If Argo had sued Jason directly in federal court, we’d look first at the constitutional limits on the federal court’s authority to compel him to litigate there. Since the federal court sits in Arizona, it seems likely that the Supreme Court would hold that the Fifth Amendment requires that Jason have sufficient minimum contacts with Arizona itself to make it fair to require him to defend there. Otherwise, the federal court might exercise jurisdiction over a defendant who had no connection whatsoever with the state in which it sat. So, even though the Fifth Amendment allows more expansive jurisdiction than the Fourteenth, I suspect that the federal courts would limit themselves to jurisdiction over defendants who have contacts with the state in which they sit. That makes sense, both because it eliminates personal jurisdiction as a forum-shopping issue between federal and state court, and because it gives parties reasonable notice about where they’ll be hailed into court. Given these considerations, let’s assume that the federal court would use Fourteenth Amendment standards to determine whether it has personal jurisdiction over Jason. Then, assuming that the federal court would use Fourteen Amendment standards, what else matters? Well, the federal court couldn’t exercise jurisdiction over Jason just because the Constitution allowed it to. It needs statutory authorization to act. And here, Rule 4(k)(1)(a) tells us that the federal court may exercise jurisdiction over Jason only if the Arizona courts could. So, the federal court will look to Arizona’s long-arm statute and ask whether it authorizes jurisdiction over Jason. If it doesn’t, the federal court cannot exercise jurisdiction either. If it does, the federal court will still need to find that it would be consistent with due process to require Jason to come to Arizona to defend the case. So B takes the prize. D suggests that the federal court could assert jurisdiction over Jason simply because he has contacts somewhere in the United States. While this is true under the Fifth Amendment, it isn’t enough to satisfy Rule 4(k)(1)(b), which ties the federal court’s jurisdictional reach to that of the state courts. E is wrong, because removal does not constitute a waiver of objections to personal jurisdiction. See Fed. R. Civ. P 8(a)(2) (‘The defenses to jurisdiction of the court must be included in the pleadings if one of them is—(A) lack of subject matter jurisdiction; (B) improper venue; (C) insufficient process; (D) insufficiency of service of process; (E) failure to join a party under Rule 19.’). C fails because the federal court looks to the Arizona long-arm statute as well as the constitution before deciding whether to exercise jurisdiction over Jason. A loses because it ignores the constitutional requirement that jurisdiction be proper as well as statutorily authorized.

Final answer: B

This question presents three possibilities about how the court will rule on the motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. A suggests that the court will find both that the long-arm statute supports jurisdiction (because Ausable ‘‘transacted business’’ there) and that it would be constitutional to assert jurisdiction over Ausable based on those contacts. B suggests that the court won’t find that Ausable ‘‘transacted business in Tennessee’’ under the long-arm statute, but leaves open whether it could constitutionally exercise jurisdiction even though the long-arm statute doesn’t authorize it. C takes the position that the court will find that the long-arm statute authorizes jurisdiction here, but that it couldn’t constitutionally exercise jurisdiction anyway. Which of these seems most plausible? Let’s start by considering whether the long-arm statute reaches Ausable. Under the statute, the court may exercise jurisdiction where the cause of action arises from the defendant’s ‘‘transaction of business’’ in Tennessee. Did Ausable ‘‘transact business’’ in Tennessee? Well, it didn’t send anyone there; it didn’t own property there; it didn’t enter contracts directly with customers there. However, it entered into a distribution agreement with Sunday River, who agreed to market Ausable products in four states, including Tennessee. And Sunday River did sell quite a few Ausable motors in Tennessee—twelve to Delta alone! So, while Ausable itself never set foot in Tennessee, it clearly anticipated selling its products there through its distributor. This indirect contact should suffice to bring Ausable within the ‘‘transacting business’’ prong of the long-arm statute. Thus, B isn’t right—the long-arm statute probably applies here. That leaves us between A and C. Both agree that the long-arm statute authorizes the assertion of jurisdiction over Ausable, but disagree about whether it would be constitutional to do so. I think we’ve seen enough examples now to know that it would be constitutional to require Ausable to defend this lawsuit in Tennessee. After all, it knew that its distributors were marketing its product there, and it received profits from those sales. Surely, it should reasonably anticipate being haled back to Tennessee to defend suits arising from those sales. So, I’d go with A. Now consider this variation:

Final answer: A
