outputs.raw: This one isn’t too hard; B wins again. If Ito had failed to appear in the Emporia action, he could raise lack of personal jurisdiction as a collateral attack on the judgment in his home forum. But here, he did appear—specially—to litigate the issue of personal jurisdiction. And he lost! Having done so, he cannot relitigate the issue collaterally in Acadia. His only recourse would have been to defend on the merits after losing the motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. By choosing instead to default, he waived any further right to contest the Emporia court’s exercise of jurisdiction over him. A suggests that Ito might still get a day in court on this issue, through an appeal in Acadia. Not true. An appellate court hears appeals from judgments entered below. Here there hasn’t even been a judgment yet in Acadia. C also fails, because Ito’s special appearance does not preserve his right to relitigate the issue later. It simply allows him to litigate it immediately, rather than waiting until the plaintiff seeks to enforce the judgment elsewhere. Once he loses on the point, he has no more rights left to assert on the issue. Final answer: B

This question illustrates the difference between personal jurisdiction over the original claim and personal jurisdiction over the claim to enforce a foreign judgment. The key fact is that Ito defended the original action in Emporia, lost, and now faces collection efforts in New Mexico. Since he did defend the original action, we know that the Emporia court exercised personal jurisdiction over him. It couldn’t have entered a valid judgment against him unless it had. And since it did, the New Mexico court will almost certainly enforce the judgment, even though Ito does not live in New Mexico, nor own real estate there, nor engage in business activities there. The Full Faith and Credit Clause requires New Mexico to give full force and effect to the Emporia judgment, once it determines that the Emporia court had the power to render it. Since Ito defended the case, the Emporia court clearly had the power to render it. Therefore, the New Mexico court will enter a New Mexico judgment on the Emporia judgment and allow Ervin to seize Ito’s time-share interest to pay off the judgment. D suggests that the New Mexico court might transfer the case to another forum, perhaps one in which Ito would be subject to specific in personam jurisdiction. But why would it? There’s nothing wrong with the New Mexico court hearing the case. It has personal jurisdiction over Ito for the claim to enforce the judgment, even if it wouldn’t have personal jurisdiction over him for the underlying fraud claim. C suggests that the New Mexico court might attach the time share, and send Ervin to Acadia to seek an order for its sale. Why would it do that? Again, there’s nothing wrong with the New Mexico proceeding. It has jurisdiction over Ito for the claim to establish the validity of the Emporia judgment, and can order the sale of the time share to satisfy it. A suggests that the New Mexico court would refuse to enforce the judgment if it concluded that it didn’t have personal jurisdiction over Ito for the underlying fraud claim. But again, the New Mexico court needn’t reach that question. Its job is to determine whether the Emporia court had the authority to render the judgment. Since Ito defended the case, it obviously did. B is the best answer. The New Mexico court will enter a judgment on the Emporia Judgment, and allow Ervin to sell the time share to satisfy it. Let me add just a few words about the situation in which the defendant fails to appear in the original action. Suppose that Ervin sues Ito in Emporia, and Ito ignores the summons and complaint. Ervin gets a default judgment for $50,00o. Now, suppose that Ervin tries to enforce the judgment in New Mexico, and Ito raises the objection that the Emporia court lacked personal Jurisdiction over him. How will the New Mexico court react? Probably, it will deny the objection. After all, Ito ignored the lawsuit, and let a default judgment be entered against him. Surely, he cannot collaterally attack the judgment by claiming that the court lacked jurisdiction over him. If he thought the court lacked jurisdiction, he should have moved to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction, rather than ignoring the case. Or, if he wanted to contest the merits, he should have answered the complaint. His decision to ignore the case implies acceptance of the court’s jurisdiction. Indeed, most courts hold that a defendant who allows a default judgment to be entered against her consents to the court’s jurisdiction. See, e.g., McDonald v. Mabey, Inc., 388 S.W.2d 288 (Ky. Ct. App. 1965); Smith v. Smith, 200 N.E.2d 472 (Ind. Ct. App. 1064).

Final answer: B

This question explores some variations on the basic theme of informal notice of suit. A suggests that oral notification suffices; it doesn’t. Even if Darrow did call Sadecki and tell her about the lawsuit, that wouldn’t suffice to start the clock running on Lorenzo’s time to respond. Under Rule 4, the only way to dispense with formal service is to use the procedure set out in Rule 4(d): sending a written request for waiver along with a copy of the complaint. B also fails. Although Darrow complied with the requirement of mailing a copy of the complaint with his request for waiver, he didn’t include a summons. Rule 4(d)(1) requires him to enclose both the summons and the complaint with the request for waiver. C works. Here, Darrow properly included the summons and complaint with his request for waiver. When Lorenzo signs the waiver form and returns it to Darrow, he has consented to jurisdiction over himself personally and submitted to the authority of the court to hear the case. No further steps need be taken to establish personal jurisdiction over him. D is close, but no cigar. True enough, the green card indicates that someone accepted delivery from the postman. However, there is nothing here indicating that Lorenzo actually received the documents or agreed to submit to the court’s jurisdiction. If he never got them, how could he agree? And even if he did get them, he hasn’t indicated that he agrees to let the case go forward. So, we’ll take C.

Final answer: C

The key here is to remember that service of process and personal jurisdiction are distinct requirements. Both must be satisfied before the court may proceed against either party. A is wrong because, although service would probably be sufficient under Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(h)(1) (B), since the method used complies with the forum’s long-arm statute, personal jurisdiction isn’t proper over either defendant. There’s nothing about this suit that arises out of activities of Preferred or Donitz in the forum state. C is also wrong. Although service might well comply with Rule 4(e)(2)(A) (since the method used is authorized by Indiana law), personal jurisdiction still wouldn’t be proper over either defendant. D fails as well. While service on Preferred would likely satisfy due process standards, since it was made pursuant to a valid state service-of-process statute, see Milliken v. Meyer, 311 U.S. 457 (1940), personal jurisdiction still doesn’t lie over Preferred. Again, none of the claims arise from anything Preferred did in Kentucky. And while personal jurisdiction would be proper over Donitz—he clearly purposefully availed himself of the privilege of conducting activities in Indiana by living there—the service on him is insufficient. Under Rule 4(k)(1)(A), service on individuals must generally be made within the district where the court sits. Here, the court sits in Kentucky, so service on Donitz in Indiana won’t do. So E takes the prize. None of these scenarios will allow the court to exercise jurisdiction over both parties.

Final answer: E

This one isn’t too hard once you’ve read the discussion above. Zirkhov sued two defendants, both of whom live outside the Northern District of Illinois. Under 28 U.S.C.§1391(b), none of the three subsections authorizes venue based solely on the residence of a codefendant. So, the Northern District of Illinois is clearly an improper venue. That means that Pardee’s motion to dismiss for improper venue is well taken. But what will the court do? A suggests that it must grant the motion to dismiss because no request to transfer has been made. Not true; the court has discretion to transfer the case anyway, under §1406(a). C takes the position that the court must transfer the case to the Western District of Kentucky, since it is a proper venue. Nope again. While the Western District of Kentucky is a proper venue, the court does not have to transfer the case there. It has discretion either to dismiss or to transfer. D argues that the court cannot transfer here, because §1406(a) doesn’t allow transfer to any district, just those in which the case ‘could have been brought,’ i.e., proper venues. True enough, but the Western District of Kentucky is a district in which the case could have been brought. E asserts that the court could transfer the case under §1404(a). Wrong again. Section 1404 only authorizes transfer of actions that were properly filed in the transferor district, while this one wasn’t. B wins, since the court has the power to transfer the case to the Western District under §1406(a).

Final answer: B

This question illustrates how much can go wrong on one little exam question! Let’s start with A. It suggests that venue will lie wherever the defendant is subject to personal jurisdiction. This isn’t true. Personal jurisdiction and venue are separate concepts. Just because you have personal jurisdiction over a party doesn’t mean that venue lies where you brought the case. For example, if you sue a California resident in Texas based on her activities in Texas, you clearly have specific in personam jurisdiction over her. But venue would still not be proper in Texas unless some other provision of the venue statute applied. So A is wrong. B also fails. Under §1391(c), a natural person resides in the district where they maintain their dwelling. Lenoir dwells in the Southern District of New York (assuming that the Southern District includes Manhattan). But what about Sorrel? She maintains her dwelling in Pittsburgh, which is presumably within the Western District of Pennsylvania. Thus, she does not reside in the Southern District of New York. Since neither defendant resides in the Southern District of New York—only Lenoir does—the residence-based venue statute won’t support venue here either. C asserts that venue is only proper in the Western District. That seems plausible, given that Sorrel resides there and Lenoir is subject to general in personam jurisdiction there. But D takes the cake. It says that no federal district has proper venue. Is that true? Well, let’s see. We’ve already seen that none of the three subsections of §1391(b) apply. What about subsection (d)? It provides that, if no other subsection applies, venue is proper in any judicial district in which any defendant is subject to personal jurisdiction at the time the action is brought. In this case, Sorrel is subject to personal jurisdiction in the Southern District of New York at the time the action is filed, because she is served with process there. Therefore, venue is proper in the Southern District of NY under §1391(d). So D is wrong too. That leaves . . . nothing. All four choices seem wrong. How could that happen? Well, it happened because Congress amended the venue statute in 2011, and changed the language of §1391(d). Before the amendment, the section provided that, if no other subsection applied, venue was proper in any district in which any defendant is found. Now, however, the section requires that the defendant be subject to personal jurisdiction in the forum district. And that means that D is now right. If Congress had left well enough alone, C would have been the best choice. But it didn’t. So, alas, D wins. Final answer: D

This question involves two different issues about how a federal court should deal with changing state law. First, what standard should govern the application of state substantive law by a federal court sitting in diversity jurisdiction? Second, can a party seek modification of a final judgment because the state supreme court has changed its interpretation of state law since the lower court rendered judgment?

The first issue is easily resolved under the principles established in York v. Guelfuccio, 682 F.3d 194 (7th Cir. 2012), which held that ‘‘the general rule . . . is that a federal court deciding a diversity case applies the law of the state as declared by the highest court of the state.’’ Id., at 195–196; see also Commins v. Pak-Mor Mfg. Co., 682 F.2d 85, 87 n.1 (1st Cir. 1982); Wright & Miller §170. In this example, the Emporia Supreme Court has spoken on the issue of joint versus several liability. Therefore, the federal appellate court should follow that pronouncement, even though the trial judge made her own prediction of Emporia law prior to the Emporia Supreme Court’s holding. So A takes the prize over B here. But wait! There’s more. What about Gleason’s motion for relief from the judgment entered against him? He didn’t appeal, but he wants out of the judgment anyway, now that we know that the trial judge misapplied Emporia law. Can he get relief from judgment without appealing? Probably not. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(1) allows parties to move for relief from judgment due to ‘‘mistake’’—but only within one year—and only where there hasn’t been an appeal. Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(c)(1). Since Gleason did not take an appeal, he cannot use Rule 60(b) to reopen the judgment. See generally Wright & Miller §2857. Thus C is wrong too. A wins again.

Final answer: A

This question tests your understanding of how a federal court chooses among competing state laws in a diversity case. A suggests that the federal court will always apply the law of the place of injury. This isn’t true; the federal court applies the law of the forum state, here Rhode Island, to determine what body of tort law to apply. C takes us half-way there. True, the federal court sitting in Rhode Island will apply Rhode Island law . . . but only to make the choice-of-law decision. B reflects the position that the federal court will simply balance the interests of the parties and states itself, without reference to any particular state’s choice-of-law rules. Not quite. Under Klaxon, the federal court will use the choice-of-law rules of Rhode Island to make the choice-of-law determination. D gets it exactly right. The federal court will ask, ‘If this case arose in a Rhode Island state court, what body of tort law would it apply?’ And then it will follow the lead of the Rhode Island state court. Here, Rhode Island’s choice-of-law rule looks to the place of the injury, so the federal court will likely conclude that the Rhode Island state court would apply Vermont law to the case. So, the federal court will too. Note that, if the case had been filed in federal court in Vermont instead, the result could easily differ. Under Klaxon, the Vermont federal court would use Vermont’s choice-of-law rules to select the governing tort law. Those rules involve a balancing process, which might lead the Vermont federal court to apply either Vermont or Rhode Island law to the case. So, once again, we see that the outcome of a diversity case may depend on where you file it, because the federal court will use the choiceof-law rules of the state in which the federal court sits to select the appropriate body of state law to apply to the case.

Final answer: D

This question asks you to consider whether Congress has the power to establish its own limitations periods for suits based on federal claims. A suggests that Congress does have this power, but only if it doesn’t abridge, enlarge or modify a substantive right under the Rules Enabling Act. But we know from Hanna that the REA does not limit Congress’s power to prescribe procedural requirements for federal court litigation; rather, it authorizes the Supreme Court to adopt such procedures. So A is wrong. B also fails, since Hanna makes clear that the potential for forum-shopping and inconsistent results among different tribunals cannot prevent application of a validly-enacted procedural requirement. D takes us back to Byers v. McAuley, where the Court held that a local statute of limitations applied to actions on federal causes of action. However, Byers predates Hanna, and Hanna clearly rejects the reasoning of Byers. Under Hanna, the fact that the limitations period affects the parties’ rights and obligations does not mean that it is beyond the reach of Congress’s rulemaking power. C is the best answer here. Since the FDLA establishes a reasonable time period for bringing suit, and since it can rationally be characterized as a matter of procedure, Congress has the power to apply it in federal court diversity cases. Thus, the federal court must dismiss Sanchez’s case, even though he could still bring his claim in state court. Note that the analysis might well differ if Congress established a longer limitations period for federal diversity cases than the states provide. It seems likely that the Court would hold that Congress lacks the power to expand the time available to sue in federal court beyond what the state provides. After all, the state creates the underlying cause of action, and presumably intends that it be enforced according to state limitations periods. On the other hand, the argument for allowing Congress to shorten the limitations period is stronger, since there is no reason to assume that the state legislature intended to preempt the federal government from limiting access to federal court through shorter limitations periods. Indeed, one might argue that the state legislatures implicitly consented to such regulation of access to federal court when they ratified the Constitution, which created the federal judiciary. This point is discussed further below.

Final answer: C

This question illustrates the importance of starting your analysis by determining what kind of conflict you face. Here, we have a conflict between a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure and state law. Therefore, the Hanna Part II analysis applies. We need to determine whether the Federal Rule is valid, that is, whether the Court had the power to promulgate it. To do that, we must determine whether the Rule is procedural, under the Sibbach definition, and does not abridge, enlarge, nor modify any substantive right, under §2072(b) of the REA. Let’s look at each option. D takes the position that the Rule is invalid, because it interferes with a substantive right. What substantive right does it interfere with? Well, perhaps the right to a unified trial! But that isn’t really a substantive right; it’s a procedural right. Or maybe the right to recover full compensation for one’s injuries? But the bifurcation didn’t prevent Columbus from recovering full compensation for her injuries, if they were caused by Moriarty. She simply failed to prove that they were. Bifurcating the trial doesn’t change the measure of recovery, or the elements of proof necessary to establish liability. It merely changes the way the issues are tried. Thus, it seems unlikely that the Rule abridges a substantive right. C argues that the state requirement of a unified trial trumps the Federal Rule, because it is contained in the state constitution. But the Supremacy Clause makes clear that federal statutes take precedence over inconsistent provisions in state constitutions. U.S. Const., Art. VI, cl. 2. So, if the Federal Rule is valid, it will trump the state constitutional provision. A asserts that the federal court erred in using the bifurcated trial, because it led to a different result than would have occurred under state law. But Hanna rejected the outcome-determinative test for challenges to Federal Rules. Instead, the question is whether the Court properly exercised its delegated legislative powers in writing the Rule. Since the Rule is valid, it controls, even if it produces a different result than state law. So B is the winner. The fact that the Rule is valid means that it is binding on the federal court, and preempts contrary state law, including state constitutional provisions. Final answer: B

This question illustrates how complex joinder can get once parties start asserting counterclaims and crossclaims. Let’s take them one at a time. First, Jasper’s claim against Holmes for the reasonable value of his services is clearly a permissible counterclaim; it arises out of the same transaction or occurrence—the creation of the Holmes software—as Holmes’s claim against Clear Code. So D is wrong on this score. But what about Jasper’s defamation claim? That also arose out of the Holmes project, since it involved statements made by Holmes during the performance of the contract. Thus, both of Jasper’s claims against Holmes arise out of the same underlying events, but neither is based on the contract between Holmes and Clear Code. Under Rule 13(h), Jasper could assert either without leave of court, even though neither would be a true counterclaim. However, he cannot assert both without leave of court, since they do not arise out of the same transaction or occurrence. So C takes the prize here. B fails too, since both of Jasper’s claims against Clear Code are proper. Both arise out of the same transaction or event—Jasper’s preparation of the Holmes program—and thus satisfy the common-nucleus test. One is a true counterclaim, arising directly out of Holmes’s claim against Clear Code, while the other is a crossclaim, arising indirectly out of Holmes’s claim. Either might lead to inconsistent results if litigated separately, so both are appropriate under Rule 18(a). A loses as well, however, because Jasper’s claim against High Tech isn’t a proper impleader claim. Impleader allows a defendant to bring in someone else who shares liability with her for the plaintiff’s injury. Here, Jasper seeks contribution from High Tech for any liability he incurs to Clear Code. This is a classic case for contribution, but not for impleader. To use impleader, Jasper would have to be a defendant in the main action, and he isn’t. Instead, he will probably want to sue High Tech in a separate suit, or perhaps add High Tech as a co-defendant through joinder of additional defendants under Rule 20(a).

Final answer: C

This is a toughie, isn’t it? Let’s start at the beginning. We need to identify each of the claims described in the question as either a counterclaim, a crossclaim, or something else. To make sense of this, draw a chart showing the parties and the claims being made. Start with the initial claim, Skolnick v. Iannotti & Erskine & Maria. Then list the subsequent claims, identifying the claimant, the defendant(s), what type of claim it is, and how it fits within Rules 13 and 14. Let’s take them one at a time. Erskine’s claim against Ian-notti is easy. It is a claim by a defendant against a codefendant, asserting that Iannotti should contribute to any recovery Skolnick gets against Erskine. Since it is a claim by a defendant against another defendant, it is clearly a crossclaim. That eliminates B, which calls it a counterclaim. D says that Erskine’s claim is a crossclaim, which is true, but goes on to say that Nickles’s claim is a crossclaim as well. Is it? Nickles is a defendant in the action, having been brought in by Maria. Skolnick’s claim against him is a claim by the plaintiff against a defendant, so it is not a crossclaim. It is a counterclaim, since it is a claim by the plaintiff against someone who has asserted a claim against him (Maria). So D is wrong. C says that Skolnick’s claim against Nick-les is a counterclaim, which is true, but adds that Iannotti’s second claim against Skolnick is a crossclaim. Is it? Nope. After Erskine brings in Iannotti, Iannotti becomes a ‘‘defending party’’ on Erskine’s claim. Thus, any claim that Iannotti makes against Erskine is a counterclaim. His second claim is a counterclaim, not a crossclaim. So C is wrong. That leaves A, which correctly labels Erskine’s claim a crossclaim, and Iannotti’s two claims counterclaims. It also correctly notes that Skolnick’s claim against Ni-kles is a counterclaim, leaving Nickles’s claim against Skol nick unclassified. What is it? It is a crossclaim, since it is a claim against a coparty. Both Skolnick and Nickles are defendants in the action after Maria brings in Nickles. So Nickles’s claim against Skollick is a crossclaim. But A doesn’t say that, though it doesn’t contradict itself by saying that it isn’t. It merely omits to classify Nickles’s claim. Since none of the others is accurate, A wins.   One last note before moving on. Notice that the court will have supplemental jurisdiction over most of these claims, since they arise out of the same events as Skolnick’s claim against Iannotti and Erskine. See 28 U.S.C.§1367(c).

Final answer: A

This question illustrates how important it is to read carefully before answering. A quick glance at the facts might lead you to conclude that the court couldn’t hear Cavers’s claim against Newcomb, since both are citizens of Wisconsin. But look again. Cavers sued Pariah on a valid federal claim, so the court clearly has original jurisdiction over the case. Since it does, it has supplemental jurisdiction over the claim against the impleaded party, Newcomb, unless §1367(b) prevents it. B suggests that the court could hear the claim anyway, because Cavers and Newcomb are from different states. They aren’t—they’re both from Wisconsin—and even if they were diverse, the court wouldn’t necessarily have jurisdiction over the claim. Supplemental jurisdiction is a statutory grant of authority, not a constitutional requirement. Even if the claim arises out of the same case or controversy as another properly asserted claim, the court still needs a statutory basis to hear it. Here, the court has supplemental jurisdiction over the claim, because it arises out of the same case or dispute as the main claim, under §1367(a); it is a direct claim between two parties already involved in the litigation arising out of the same events as the main claim. C takes the position that the court could hear the claim simply because it meets the Gibbs standard for a single constitutional case. That’s true, but irrelevant here. The court won’t hear the claim absent a statutory basis for doing so. D argues that the court has supplemental jurisdiction over the added claim, and that §1367(b)—the limitation on supplemental jurisdiction in diversity cases—doesn’t bar it. Wrong. Although the court has supplemental jurisdiction over the new claim under §1367( a), §1367(b) prohibits the court from hearing it. The case is based solely on diversity? No, it’s based on a federal question claim. Wait, wait, wait! How about the claim against Newcomb? Is that based on diversity? Yes, but §1367(b) only limits supplemental jurisdiction where the underlying case is based solely on diversity. Here, the underlying case is based on a federal claim, so §1367(b) doesn’t apply. A is right. The court has supplemental jurisdiction over Cavers’s claim against Newcomb under §1 367(a), but §1367(b)’s restriction on supplemental jurisdiction in diversity cases doesn’t apply, since the underlying case is based on a valid federal claim. So the court should hear the claim. Note that, although the claim against Newcomb is based on diversity, the case itself is not, since it includes a valid independent federal claim. Consequently, §1367(b)’ s limitations do not apply. One more point: Suppose that Cavers had sued Pariah on a state law claim, and that Pariah had impleaded Newcomb. Could Cavers then bring a claim against Newcomb? Probably not. See Finley v. United States, 490 U.S. 545 (1989).

Final answer: A

This question requires you to parse the statutory language very carefully. Let’s start with A. It suggests that the district court has supplemental jurisdiction over Westford’s claim, but that this jurisdiction is barred by §1369(b). That section provides that ‘‘the district courts shall not hear . . . other [supplemental] claims’’ if they arise from different common nucleus of operative fact from the main claim. Here, both plaintiffs’ claims clearly arise out of the same employment relationship, so their claims do arise from the same core facts. So §1367(b) doesn’t bar supplemental jurisdiction here; A takes us down the wrong path. B argues that there isn’t supplemental jurisdiction over Westford’s claim. But §1367(a) says that, where the court has original jurisdiction over some claims, it may exercise supplemental jurisdiction over any other claims arising from the same case or controversy. Here, the court has original jurisdiction over Cavers’s claim, and Westford’s arises from the same case or controversy—so how can we say that the court lacks supplemental jurisdiction? C asserts that the court has supplemental jurisdiction over Westfords claim, and that it is not barred by §1367b). This seems right. D is the most interesting choice. It suggests that the court cannot take supplemental jurisdiction over Westford’s claim even though §1367(a) authorizes it to do so, because Westford’s claim fails to meet the amount-in-controversy requirement of §1332(a)(I). Before the enactment of §1367, this argument would have been persuasive. As noted above, before the supplemental jurisdiction statute, the rule was that each plaintiff had to establish an independent basis for subject matter jurisdiction. Thus, if two plaintiffs joined in a suit, each had to show that she satisfied all three elements of §1332(a): citizenship, amount in controversy, and arisal of the claim in diversity. And, if two defendants were sued, the plaintiff had to make out a separate case for diversity jurisdiction against each defendant. Section 1367 changed that. By providing that, once the court has original jurisdiction over some of the claims in the action, it will generally have supplemental jurisdiction over others, it eliminated the need for each party to establish an independent basis for subject-matter jurisdiction. Once the court has original jurisdiction over some claim, it will usually have supplemental jurisdiction over related ones, without regard to whether they themselves provide an independent basis for subject matter jurisdiction under Article III or §1332. So, while Westford’s claim itself wouldn’t support diversity jurisdiction, it can still be heard through supplemental jurisdiction, because Cavers’s claim supports diversity jurisdiction. The point of supplemental jurisdiction is to allow parties to join additional claims without having to worry about meeting jurisdictional requirements for each one. So C wins.

Final answer: C

This question illustrates how important it is to understand the requirements of the pleading rules before responding to a complaint. A is wrong because Rule 8(b)(2) does not authorize partial admissions and denials; it requires that the defendant either admit or deny the entire allegation. B is also wrong, because the defendant cannot simply ignore an allegation in the complaint. Failure to deny an allegation constitutes an express admission under Rule 8(b)(6). C suggests that AE could avoid taking a position on the issue by stating that it lacks sufficient information to form a belief about the allegation. But this won’t work either. While Rule 8(b)(5) authorizes a party who truly lacks information to state that fact, here AE has some information supporting the allegation and some contradicting it. It knows enough to challenge the allegation, though perhaps not enough to prove that it is false. So D is the best choice. Since AE denies that Adair acted within the scope of employment, the allegation remains in controversy between the parties, and Patterson will have to go forward with proof to establish it. Even if AE later discovers that Adair was acting in the course of employment after all, it still has denied the allegation, and Patterson will have to prove it anyway. Of course, AE could always amend its answer to withdraw the denial, but it probably wouldn’t want to do that. Once it has learned that Adair was acting in the line of duty, it presumably wants to argue that Patterson’s own negligence contributed to cause the accident, rather than arguing that Adair wasn’t acting in the scope of employment. In any event, once it has denied the allegation, it will likely lose the ability to amend its answer to withdraw the denial. See Fed. R. Civ. P .15(a)(1)(B).

Final answer: D

This question illustrates how the pleading rules work together to help define the disputed issues between the parties. A is wrong because, although the police report supports the allegation, Lopes does not know whether there were other witnesses whose accounts differ. He cannot properly admit the allegation unless he knows it is true; otherwise, he risks having it taken as established fact under Rule 8(c). B is also wrong. It is true that Lopes will probably want to contest the allegation at trial, but he cannot simply deny every allegation in the complaint that he hopes to challenge later. Rule 8(b)(2) provides that denials must ‘‘fairly meet the substance of the challenged allegations,’’ meaning that the defendant must deny only those allegations that she disputes. D is also improper here. Rule 8(b)(6) makes clear that failure to deny an allegation constitutes an admissions of its truth. So, if Lopes fails to respond to Paragraph 21, he admits that Hooper signaled. That leaves C, which is the best choice. Since Lopes lacks personal knowledge of the signaling issue, and has insufficient information to assess the reliability of the witness quoted in the police report, he should say so. This preserves his ability to investigate further and to contest the allegation later if he finds reason to doubt its accuracy. And, importantly, it puts Cardozo on notice that Lopes intends to contest the allegation, rather than conceding it. In practice, plaintiffs often fail to pay close attention to the defendant’s responses to allegations in the complaint. But careful comparison of the complaint and answer can save considerable effort down the road. For example, if Lopes had admitted that Hooper signaled, then Cardozo could assume that point was conceded, and focus on proving other elements of his case. Or, if Lopes denied the allegation, Cardozo would know that he needed to prove that Hooper signaled in order to recover. By responding that he lacked sufficient information to form a belief about it, Lopes indicates that he contests the allegation, but hasn’t investigated enough to confirm or refute it. Thus, Cardozo still needs to prove that Hooper signaled, though he may hope that Lopes won’t pursue the matter vigorously once he learns that there is some evidence supporting it. Of course, the plaintiff may choose to ignore the defendant’s responses altogether, and proceed to develop proof on all allegations in the complaint. However, where the defendant has responded carefully—and honestly—to the allegations in the complaint, the plaintiff ignores the answer at her peril. The next question involves another aspect of the defendant’s response to the plaintiff’s allegations.

Final answer: C

This question illustrates how difficult these cases can get. Let’s start with B; it fails because White did receive sufficient notice within the limitations period. True, he didn’t know that Williams was going to sue him personally. However, he knew that someone had sued another officer at the station house for using excessive force in making an arrest. And he knew that the arrest described in the lawsuit was the very arrest in which he participated. Given those two pieces of information, isn’t it fair to say that White ‘‘should have known that the action would have . . . been brought against [him]?’’ Rule 15(c)(l)(c)(ii). I think so. He certainly could have figured out that Williams might realize that he was the real culprit, and bring an amended complaint naming him instead of Black. Thus, C is wrong too. White did have sufficient notice within the limitations period that he was the intended target of the suit. That leaves us between A and D. Both make valid points. D is true: The amended allegation does arise out of the same event—the arrest—as the original complaint. But A is also true: The amendment was made well beyond the limitations period. Which takes precedence? Here again, the rulemakers have provided guidance. They’ve said that, where the amendment changes parties, all three conditions of Rule 15(c)(l )(C) must be met. Since the amendment here was not made until long after the limitations period ran, it cannot relate back. Final answer: A

Final answer: A

This question illustrates how difficult it sometimes is to determine what issues the parties have actually litigated. A is wrong because, although evidence regarding Jhala’s use of the ORV was introduced at trial, it was introduced solely to prove the issue of comparative negligence. It certainly doesn’t follow from the introduction of such evidence that the parties implicitly agreed to try the additional issue of assumption of the risk. B is also wrong; the failure to plead an issue does not necessarily preclude a party from relying upon it later. Under Rule 15(b), the court has discretion to allow an amendment to include an issue that the parties have actually litigated, even if it wasn’t included in the original pleading. But C isn’t right either. Although the parties here litigated the issue of comparative negligence, there is nothing to suggest that they litigated the separate issue of assumption of the risk. Thus D is the best choice. Since the parties didn’t litigate the assumption-of-the-risk issue, the court shouldn’t allow an amendment adding it to the answer, nor should it instruct the jury on it. The parties litigated the issue of comparative fault, but not the distinct issue of assumption of the risk. So the fact that they litigated the former issue does not imply that they litigated the latter. The difference between this question and Question 3 above is that, in Question 3, the parties litigated two different claims—they developed evidence supporting both a contract claim and a quantum meruit claim—and thus could be said to have litigated both. Here, however, the parties litigated only one issue, comparative negligence, and the mere development of evidence on that issue cannot be taken to indicate that they intended to litigate another issue, assumption of the risk, as well. The following question involves a slightly different twist on the theme of implied litigation of unpleaded issues.

Final answer: D

This question tests your understanding of who can be sanctioned under Rule 11, which actions give rise to liability under Rule 11, and the procedures for imposing sanctions under Rule 11. A is wrong because Rule 11 authorizes sanctions only against attorneys, unrepresented parties, or parties represented by attorneys. Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(a). So the client cannot be sanctioned for filing the complaint. B is wrong too; it suggests that the entire firm can be sanctioned for the act of one partner. Again, Rule 11(a) authorizes sanctions only against the attorney responsible for the violation, the party she represents, or an unrepresented party. C is right. Rule 11(c)(1)(A) authorizes the imposition of appropriate sanctions upon the party or attorney who violates Rule 11. Sanctions may consist of an order to pay a penalty into court, or to pay part of the opposing side’s fees, or any other appropriate sanction. An order directing the offending attorney to attend CLE training seems within the range of permissible sanctions. D is wrong. While the failure to respond fully to a document request is certainly improper conduct, it isn’t a violation of Rule 11. Rule 37 governs responses to requests for production of documents. E is wrong. Although Norris’s representation to the court is false, it doesn’t violate Rule 11. Rule 5.2 of the Model Rules of Professional Conduct prohibits such representations, and Rule 3.3(a)(3) requires correction of them once discovered. But Rule 11 applies only to written submissions to the court. See Fed. R. Civ. P .11(a). F is wrong. Rule 11(c)(2) provides that a party wishing to seek sanctions under Rule 11 must serve a motion for sanctions on the offending party. Here, the defendant didn’t make a motion for sanctions, though he easily could have done so. Without a motion, the court lacks authority to impose sanctions under Rule 11. Thus, C is the best choice.

Final answer: C

This one should be pretty straightforward. D is wrong, because this is a removed case; state procedure governs until removal. So the fact that Rule 12 allows a defendant to combine several defenses in a pre-answer motion doesn’t matter here. C is also wrong, because again, this is a removed case, and state procedure controls until removal. Under state procedure (in our hypothetical), the special appearance approach applies, not Rule 12. So the fact that Rule 20(a) allows a defendant to include several defenses in an answer won’t save Hue. He didn’t file an answer at all! He made a special appearance to challenge jurisdiction, then moved to dismiss for another reason. This constitutes a general appearance under the special appearance doctrine, so B takes the prize. A is clearly wrong as well. Removing a case from state court to federal court does not constitute a submission to the federal court’s jurisdiction. Rather, it asserts the right to proceed there instead of in state court. See Chapter 3, p. 74.

Final answer: B

This one should be pretty straightforward. D is wrong; the special appearance rule doesn’t govern here. Once this case is removed to federal court, the Federal Rules control. So the fact that the state court would use the special appearance approach is irrelevant. A is also wrong. Under Rule 8(a), the proper method of removing a case is to file a notice of removal. No other papers need accompany the notice of removal. However, nothing prevents the defendant from filing other documents at the time of removal (or soon thereafter). Here, Hue didn’t raise his jurisdictional objection in the notice of removal, but he did raise it promptly afterward—in his answer—before any further steps were taken in the litigation. B takes the cake. This choice suggests that, since Hue answered on the merits as well as asserting two Rule 12(b) defenses, he has waived his objection to personal jurisdictions. Not true! Under Rule 12(h)(2), a defendant may raise more than one defense in her initial responsive pleading without losing any of them. C is right. Since the parties will proceed under the Federal Rules now that the case has been removed, the special appearance rule won’t apply. Instead, they’ll follow Rule 12, which allows a defendant to combine several defenses in her first response to the complaint. Goloupolos v. Hue, 307 F.Supp. 645 (N.D.Cal. 1970); see also Wright & Miller §1352.

Final answer: C

This question illustrates how the work product doctrine operates to protect certain materials from discovery, while leaving others subject to compelled disclosure. Let’s start with D. This suggests that the tape is discoverable under Rule 26( b)(3)(C), because it includes the statement of a witness. This isn’t quite accurate; the subpart cited doesn’t exist! There is no exception to work product protection for statements of witnesses. Nor does the fact that the tape contains a witness’s statement mean that it is not protected by the work product doctrine. The tape is a document, prepared by or for Mason, in anticipation of litigation. Therefore, it qualifies as ‘‘trial preparation material’’ under Rule 26(b)( 3)(A), and is presumptively protected from discovery. So B fails too. Even though Drake needs the testimony of Collins, and presumably could not get his version without taking his deposition, the tape is still protected from discovery. It reveals the substance of what Collins told Mason’s counsel during the investigation of the case. Since it was obtained by Mason’s counsel in the process of investigating the case, it is likely to reflect Mason’s assessment of the strength of the evidence against Drake, and thus to disclose the mental impressions of counsel. See Fed. R. Civ. P 26(b)(3)(i). Consequently, it falls into the category of materials that are protected from disclosure even where there is a substantial need for them. So C takes the prize here. Mason must identify Collins as a potential witness, since the interrogatory asks only for the name of anyone who may know something about the accident. It does not ask for details of what those people said. And Mason’s counsel did take the statement of a person who may have seen the fire begin. While the content of that statement is protected from disclosure, the existence of the statement—and the identity of the person making it—is not. So Mason must respond to the interrogatory. On the other hand, the tape itself is protected from disclosure under Rule 22(b)(3)(B), since it reveals the contents of the witness’s statement, and thus the mental impressions of counsel. Note that the result would be different if Drake served a subpoena duces tecum on Collins himself, requiring him to appear before Drake’s counsel and give his account of the fire. Collins would very likely have to testify, since he is not represented by counsel, and the subpoena would require him to provide information in his possession, not the work product of counsel. Of course, if Drake deposed Collins directly, he’d learn whatever Collins knows anyway. But Mason’s counsel won’t be forced to turn over the fruits of his investigative labors.

Final answer: C

This question illustrates how the work-product doctrine operates outside the context of requests for production of documents. Here, DeMarco wants to ask questions about the content of communications between Sanchez and her lawyer during the course of litigation. These communications clearly constitute ‘‘trial preparation material,’’ since they involve discussions between client and counsel in anticipation of litigation. They also reflect the mental processes of counsel in preparing for the deposition. Under Hickman, such materials are protected from discovery, even if they do not fall squarely within the ambit of Rule 26(b)(3). A is wrong here; the attorney-client privilege protects confidential communications between clients and attorneys, but only where those communications concern legal advice given by the attorney. Communications between client and counsel that don’t seek or convey legal advice aren’t covered by the privilege. Here, the communication appears to consist of discussion of facts, not legal advice. B is also weak. While the information sought certainly constitutes ‘‘trial preparation material,’’ it doesn’t take the form of a ‘‘document or tangible thing.’’* C fails too. As discussed above, intangible work product remains protected under Hickman, even if Rule 26( b)(3) does not apply. E is also off base. Even if Rule 26(b)( 3 ) did not apply, the information requested could still be protected from discovery under Hickman. D is right. Since the information reflects the thought processes of counsel, it is opinion work product, and thus protected from discovery under Hickman, regardless of whether Rule 26(b)(3)’s requirements are met. *The Federal Rules Advisory Committee considered adding language to Rule 26(b)(3)(A) protecting oral work product, but decided against doing so. See Advisory Committee Note to 2000 Amendment to Rule 26(b)(4).

Final answer: D

This question illustrates the importance of understanding the purpose of each step in litigation. Here, D is wrong; Roh does not need to be a party to be deposed. She is a potential witness whose knowledge is relevant to the issues in dispute between the parties. B suggests that Czonka’s lawyer should resist NorthStar’s efforts to depose Roh until later in the case, when she would presumably know more about the facts of the case. But there is no rule requiring that depositions wait until both sides have completed investigation into the facts of the case. Indeed, the whole point of discovery is to investigate those facts. So long as the deposition is reasonably calculated to lead to discoverable information, it is proper. See Fed. R. Civ. P .26(b)(1) (‘parties may obtain discovery regarding any matter that is not privileged and is relevant to the claim or defense of any party’’). And here, Roh’s testimony clearly could lead to such information. Thus, Czonka’s counsel should expect to defend the deposition, even though it comes early in the case. C is tempting, but probably unethical. It suggests that Czonka’s counsel should agree to meet informally with Roh, outside the context of a formal deposition, to discuss the case. This might well provide valuable information about the case, but it raises serious ethical problems. Under Model Rules of Professional Conduct Rule 4.2, lawyers generally may not communicate directly with represented persons about the subject of the representation unless the lawyer receives consent from the adverse party’s lawyer. Since Roh is represented by NorthStar’s counsel, Czonka’s counsel should not contact her directly to discuss the case. To do so would violate the spirit—if not the letter—of Rule 4.2. Even if Czonka’s counsel did speak with Roh, she would still want to depose her, to preserve her testimony under oath. So C is not right either. That leaves A. Shouldn’t Czonka’s counsel save her toughest questioning for trial? Not necessarily. True, Czonka’s counsel doesn’t know much about the case at this stage, two months after filing suit. But she certainly needs to find out! And Roh is a key witness. Her testimony will almost surely reveal important evidence about whether Czonka was discriminated against. Moreover, although Czonka’s counsel hasn’t had time to develop the full picture of the case, she undoubtedly understands the basic claims and defenses in the action. She should be able to frame questions that will help her understand Roh’s role in the events leading up to Czonka’s discharge. There is nothing improper about asking probing questions during a deposition. Counsel often do so, especially where—as here—they anticipate that the witness will be hostile to their client’s position. Of course, Czonka’s counsel won’t know everything about the case when she takes Roh’s deposition. But she’ll never know anything about it if she waits until she does. Discovery is designed to fill gaps in the parties’ knowledge of the facts. Taking Roh’s deposition now will help fill those gaps. So A is the best choice.

Final answer: A

This question illustrates how the rules governing discovery often lead to broad disclosure of information, even where the information might not be admissible at trial. D is right here. Rule 30(c)(1) allows the deponent’s counsel to make objections during the deposition, but does not allow him to prevent the witness from answering unless one of three conditions is met. One condition is that the question seeks privileged matter. Another is that the court has limited the scope of the deposition through a protective order. And the third is that the deponent’s counsel moves for a protective order based on improper conduct by opposing counsel. None of those circumstances exist here. The fact that the information called for by the question would be inadmissible at trial doesn’t justify refusing to answer the question. Nor does irrelevance. It isn’t clear whether the information really is irrelevant, since it goes to Unger’s general credibility as an appraiser. But even if it is irrelevant, Rule 30(c)(2)’s language suggests that the witness should answer anyway. The rule says that the witness needn’t answer only if instructed not to by counsel, and counsel may give such instructions only in very narrow circumstances. Thus, B is wrong. A is also wrong, because the fact that the information would be inadmissible at trial as double hearsay wouldn’t ordinarily support an instruction not to answer. C fails too. While Rule 30(d)(2) does authorize an objection based on work-product protection, it doesn’t authorize the deponent’s attorney to refuse to let the witness answer. Instead, it requires the witness to answer, subject to the objection. The point of the provision is to put the burden on the party seeking the discovery to go to court to resolve the dispute over discoverability. See Fed. R. Civ. P., Advisory Committee Note to Subdivision (d)(2).

Final answer: D

This question illustrates some important points about summary judgment practice. First, D is right; C is wrong. Summary judgment is not appropriate if the moving party fails to submit evidentiary materials showing entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, even if the opponent doesn’t respond at all. Rule 56(a) requires the movant to show that there is no dispute of material fact and that she is entitled to judgment as a mater of law. If she hasn’t done this, the court cannot grant her motion without more information. So here, if the judge concludes that the note is a valid contract, she still needs more information before entering judgment for Maxwell. She would need to know what the damages were, or how much time Maxwell spent doing the work (if he seeks recovery on a quantum meruit basis). Thus, A is wrong too. Even if the judge finds that the note is a valid contract establishing liability, she will have to hold further proceedings to determine the amount of money owed. B is also wrong. If the judge concludes that the document is not a valid contract, she won’t simply throw Maxwell out of court. There could still be a trial on the claim based on quantum meruit, which does not require proof of a formal agreement between the parties. So the judge might deny the motion, or might grant partial summary judgment for Maxwell on the contract claim, leaving issues of damages to be tried later. Or, if she concludes that the note is invalid, she might grant summary judgment for Chao on the express contract claim, but leave the quantum meruit claim for trial. This shows one way in which summary judgment for the plaintiff differs from summary judgment for the defendant. When the defendant wins summary judgment, the case ends. Not necessarily true when the plaintiff prevails on summary judgment. Often, the only issues resolved by summary judgment for the plaintiff are questions of liability. Damages remain to be determined through further litigation. For example, in many personal injury cases, the plaintiff will move for summary judgment on the issue of liability after discovery closes. If granted, the jury will then hear evidence only on the issue of damages. And sometimes, the plaintiff will win summary judgment on some theories of relief, while others go forward to trial. For example, a plaintiff who sues for both negligence and strict products liability may establish that she is entitled to recover on the negligence claim, but lose summary judgment on the strict liability claim. Then, the negligence claim will be dismissed, but the strict liability claim will proceed to trial. Finally, consider this variation on the last question.

Final answer: D

This question illustrates how difficult it sometimes is to tell whether a challenge goes to the court’s power to hear the case (subject matter jurisdiction) or to the truth of the allegations made by one side or another. Here, FunSoft argues that it didn’t do something—sell Voop in Illinois—that would make it liable for trademark infringement. But this argument also implies that the court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over the case. After all, if FunSoft never sold Voop in Illinois, then Conway’s claim doesn’t arise under federal trademark law, since no act of infringement took place within the United States. So, if FunSoft’s position is true, the court will lack subject matter jurisdiction over the case. A is wrong here, however, because the court isn’t called upon to resolve factual disputes about jurisdiction using the summary judgment procedure. Instead, it resolves them directly, without regard to whether they are genuinely contested. B suggests that the court should use the summary judgment process to determine whether it has subject matter jurisdictions. This is not right either. Summary judgment is used to dispose of cases where there is insufficient evidence to support a verdict for one side or the other. But here, the court needs to know whether FunSoft actually sold Voop in Illinois before it can even consider the merits of the case. If it didn’t, the court won’t have subject matter jurisdiction over the case at all. So the court shouldn’t apply the summary judgment test to see if there is sufficient evidence to create a jury question on the point. Rather, it should simply determine whether FunSoft sold Voop there. C takes the position that the court should grant summary judgment against Conway if it concludes that FunSoft did not market Vooper in Illinois. That makes sense, but D is better still. Under Rule 56(c)(1), the court should give Conway a chance to respond to FunSoft’s showing that it did not market Voop in Illinois, just as it would if FunSoft had moved for summary judgment on the merits rather than on the issue of subject matter jurisdiction. And, once it receives any responsive materials from Conway, the court should apply the summary judgment standard to determine whether there is enough evidence to raise a reasonable inference that FunSoft did market Voop in Illinois. If there is, the court should proceed to consider the merits of the case. Only if there is no such evidence should it conclude that it lacks subject matter jurisdiction over the case and dismiss it. Note that the court might well reach the same result under both approaches. However, the proper approach is to treat the motion as one for summary judgment on the merits, allowing Conway to submit opposing materials, and applying the summary judgment standard to determine whether the case should go forward. Otherwise, the court would be deciding the ultimate issue in the case—the very thing that summary judgment is designed to avoid—in resolving the threshold issue of subject matter jurisdiction.

Final answer: D

This question illustrates one of the problems created by the Supreme Court’s holding in Baltimore & Carolina Line, which requires a party to make a pre-verdict motion for judgment as a matter of lawwithin ten days of the close of evidence—in order to renew the motion after the verdict. Here, Colon did just what the rule requires; he moved for judgment as a matter of lawafter the close of evidence, and then sought reconsideration of the jury’s verdict based on insufficient evidence. But he changed horses along the way. His first motion challenged the sufficiency of the evidence on one element—Colon’s knowledge that the representations were false—and his postverdict motion challenges another element—Uberoth’s reliance on those representations. Is this allowed? It seems doubtful that it is. Surely, the purpose of the ‘‘prior motion’’ requirement is to give notice to the other side that you believe their proof fails on some particular element of their case. That allows them to remedy any deficiency in their proof, if they can. If they don’t realize until after the verdict that they failed to prove an essential element, they won’t have a chance to fill the gap. And, even if we put aside the policy considerations behind the prior-motion requirement, I doubt that the drafters intended to require a party to anticipate every possible objection to the sufficiency of the evidence supporting each element of the plaintiff ’s case. B takes the prize here. Even though Colon complied with the formal requirements of Rule 50(b)—making a pretrial motion for judgment as a matter of l awand filing the renewal motion within twenty-eight days—the judge should reject the motion, since it raises a new argument that Uberoth’s evidence was insufficient to support a verdict. D suggests that the judge should grant the motion if she believes that no reasonable jury could find that Uberoth relied on Colon’s representations. However, the judge cannot consider whether the evidence supports the jury’s conclusion on reliance without considering all the evidence offered on that issue. She needs to hear the arguments and evaluate the evidence on that issue. She doesn’t need to hold a hearing on the issue, however. Under Rule 50(c)(1), the court may decide the motion without oral hearings. C also fails. Although the judge concluded that Uberoth presented sufficient evidence to submit the case to the jury, she might well change her mind upon reflection. Or, she might conclude that the evidence was sufficient to create a factual dispute for the jury, but that no reasonable juror could find for Uberoth on that basis. See Smith v. Kmart Corp., 171 F.3d 256, 260 n.8 (5th Cir. 1999); see generally Wright & Miller §2537. Finally, A is wrong, because the motion does not violate the timing provision of Rule 50(b). It is filed within twenty-eight days after the verdict, although before judgment has formally been entered on the verdict. Rule 50(b) clearly contemplates motions for judgment notwithstanding the verdict being filed between the return of the verdict and the entry of judgment. Indeed, the rule states that the motion shall be filed ‘’no later than . . . [twenty-eight] days after the entry of judgment.’’

Final answer: B

This question illustrates how different things look when the judge is acting as the trier of fact. In a jury trial, the judge could not grant Colon’s motion here, even if she concluded that Uberoth had not produced enough evidence to prove knowledge of falsity. That conclusion might well turn out to be mistaken, since the judge must view the evidence in the light most favorable the nonmoving party, and draw inferences in her favor. It wouldn’t be appropriate for the judge to substitute her own assessment of the evidence for that of the jury. Here, however, the judge isn’t constrained by these considerations. There is no jury to usurp, so the judge can evaluate the evidence directly, and determine whether she believes that Colon acted knowingly. A is wrong, then, because the judge needn’t limit herself to assessing whether Uberoth has met the burden of producing sufficient evidence to go to the jury. Instead, she can consider whether Uberoth has carried his ultimate burden of persuasion—whether he has convinced her, based on the evidence presented thus far, that Colon knew the representations were false. D is also wrong. True, under Rule 50(b), a party who loses after the judge submits the case to the jury may renew her motion for JMOL after the jury returns a verdict. But again, those provisions don’t apply here, since there is no jury. Nor is there any point in waiting until the close of all the evidence to ask the judge to rule on the sufficiency of the plaintiff ’s case. Since the judge is going to weigh the evidence anyway, she might as well stop the proceedings if she concludes that the plaintiff hasn’t persuaded her that Colon was guilty of fraud. C takes the cake. Under this approach, the judge would continue hearing evidence, despite concluding that the plaintiff hadn’t satisfied her that Colon committed fraud. Why would she want to waste everyone’s time like that? B is clearly the best choice. Once the judge decides that the plaintiff hasn’t proven his claim, she should just put an end to the proceeding. This is one of the advantages of having the judge try the case instead of a jury. When the judge tries the case, she can cut through the formalities associated with preserving the jury’s province, and focus on getting to the bottom of the dispute.

Final answer: B

This question tests whether you understand the effect of the trial judge’s order granting one post-trial motion and denying others. Let’s consider each option. A suggests that Parkins could immediately appeal both the grant of the JNOV and the conditional grant of the new trial. This isn’t right; the two rulings aren’t independent. Under Rule 50(c)(1) the judge grants the motion for judgment as a matter law, but also rules on the motion for a new trial, which she denies. She doesn’t mean that the plaintiff gets her choice between them! Rather, the idea is that the judgment as a matter of law takes precedence over the new trial. That is, if the judgment as a matter of law is upheld on appeal, the case ends without further proceedings. Only if the judgment as a matter of la w is reversed will the new trial take place. Thus, the grant of the new trial is contingent upon reversal of the judgment as a matter of law. Since the new trial hasn’t been ordered unconditionally, it cannot be appealed separately. B is the best answer here. C fails because the grant of the new trial is conditional, not absolute. D is tempting, but wrong. Although the new trial itself hasn’t occurred, the judge has ruled on the motion for a new trial. Her denial of that motion is a separate issue from the grant of the judgment as a matter of la . Both rulings are subject to immediate appeal, even though the new trial will never occur unless the judgment as a matter of law fails on appeal. Note that the same result would follow had the judge denied the motion for judgment as a matter o f law, but granted the motion for a new trial. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 50(c)(2). In that event, the plaintiff could still appeal the denial of the motion for judgment as a ma tter of law, while the defendant could appeal the grant of the new trial. Again, the new trial would proceed only if the judgment as a matter of l aw were affirmed on appeal. One other point about Rule 50(c): Subsection (c)(4) provides that, where the judge grants or denies any of these motions, she shall specify the reasons for doing so. This requirement helps ensure that the parties know exactly what issues they need to raise on appeal, and allows the appellate court to focus its attention on those issues. Without specific findings by the district judge, the parties might have to guess at the basis for the judge’s action, making effective appellate advocacy difficult. Moreover, the appellate court needs to know precisely what the lower court decided in order to determine whether it made a mistake. Consequently, the judge’s reasoning process must be laid bare for appellate scrutiny.

Final answer: B

This question tests whether you understand the effect of the conditional order granting a new trial. Under Rule 50(c)(2), the conditional order granting a new trial becomes effective only if the appellate court reverses the judgment as a matter of law. Since the appellate court here concluded that the trial judge erred in entering judgment as a matter of law, the conditional order granting a new trial takes effect. Thus A is wrong; the case cannot go back down for entry of a judgment for Sardinia. Nor could it go back for entry of a judgment for Knox, since the appellate court reversed the judgment as a matter of law for him. B fails too. C looks good, doesn’t it? The appellate court found error in the causation instruction, which would entitle Knox to a new trial. Why isn’t that right? Because the trial judge already ruled on that issue! She considered the argument that the causation instruction was erroneous, rejected it, and refused to grant a new trial on that basis. Her decision on that point is before the appellate court, along with her other rulings. The appellate court has decided that she made one mistake—denying the motion for judgment as a matter-of-law—but two out of three ain’t bad. They affirmed her denial of the motion for JNOV and her refusal to grant a new trial due to the causation instruction. So they don’t send the case back for a new trial. Instead, D is right—they send it back for the trial judge to enter judgment for Sardinha. This result may seem odd, since the appellate court agreed that the judge gave the wrong instruction on causation. But remember, the appellate court reviews each of the issues raised below independently. Even though the judge made one mistake, the others were proper. So the case goes back for entry of a judgment for Sardina. One last question about post-trial motions . . .

Final answer: D

This example illustrates how intersystem preclusion works. Here, Pelham sued twice, once in each system. His first case was decided by a federal court; so we start there. Under the Second Restatement approach, which governs in federal court, may Pelham bring both sets of claims in the same action? Probably yes. There is no reason why he couldn’t join his state tort claims along with his federal constitutional claim arising out of the same incident. They arise out of the same transaction or occurrence, and there is nothing about them that makes joinder improper. So C looks like the right answer here. However, let me complicate things just a bit more. Suppose instead that Pelham had lost on the merits in his first action—say, because the jury found that Correro didn’t use excessive force at all—and now wants to sue again in state court on his state law claims. Would he still be barred? I think so. Even if he hadn’t raised these claims before, he should have done so. Since he could have litigated them in the prior action, he shouldn’t get a second bite at the apple. A is wrong, since this isn’t simply a situation where the plaintiff failed to raise some claims in her first action. It’s worse than that: She could have raised those additional claims but chose not to do so. B also fails, because Pelham could have asserted his state law claims in his original action. D is wrong too, because the issue isn’t whether the state court would allow the claims together. Rather, the question is whether the federal court would bar further litigation of the state law claims, even though they were not raised earlier. And it would, because they arose out of the same events as the claims actually litigated, and could properly have been included in the first action. Once the federal court has entered a final judgment on the merits, the parties cannot go back to relitigate any other claims arising out of the same events. That’s true regardless of whether the subsequent action is filed in state or federal court. Intersystem preclusion is governed by the principle that a party gets only one shot at litigating all claims arising out of a particular dispute. Whether you file your first action in state or federal court, you’ll generally lose the opportunity to re-litigate claims arising out of the same event in a second action in the other system.

Final answer: C

This example illustrates how intersystem preclusion works. Here, the federal court should look to the preclusive effect that the Emporia state court itself would give its own judgment. Under this analysis, D is wrong; the fact that the Emporia court might allow a second action does not bar the federal court action here. Rather, the federal court asks whether the Emporia court would allow a second action by Pelham. Since it wouldn’t—because it follows the Second Restatement approach—the federal court will as well. A is wrong too, though, since the federal court isn’t applying its own claim preclusion rules directly. It is using them indirectly, by asking what result they would lead to in the Emporia court. C is also wrong. There is nothing sacrosanct about federal court jurisdiction over federal questions. Just because Congress has authorized suits in federal court doesn’t mean that a party can bring successive actions whenever there is some basis for bringing at least one of those actions in federal court. B takes the prize. Because the Emporia court would bar the subsequent §1983 action, so will the federal court.

Final answer: B

This question illustrates two important points about collateral estoppel. First, if the losing party in the earlier action wants to avoid estoppel, she will argue that the decision on the issue wasn’t really necessary to support the judgment. If the court agrees, the loser gets another chance to litigate the issue. But here, the judge clearly relied on the finding that the brochure didn’t promise a specific rate of return in deciding that Gotschall couldn’t recover. So C fails; the issue was necessary to the result in the first action. D also fails, because the court allows non-mutual estoppel in these circumstances. Since the court does allow Faithful to assert estoppel against Carmichael, you need to choose between A and B. A suggests that Carmichael should lose because he failed to join Gotschall’s lawsuit. It isn’t clear how the court could enforce such a rule. How would it know that other investors might want to sue? And what remedy would it impose if they didn’t join the first suit? Surely, it won’t refuse to hear their claims! Thus, A is wrong. That leaves B, which correctly states that the court will bar Carmichael from relitigating the issue, even though he was not a party to the first action. The fact that the issue was litigated and decided in the first action, and was necessary to the outcome in that action, supports application of estoppel. Note that the analysis doesn’t depend on whether the court applies mutual or non-mutual estoppel rules. Even under mutuality, where only parties to the first action may invoke estoppel, the court would grant summary judgment for Faithful. Why? Because Faithful itself litigated the issue in the first action, and lost. Under mutuality, Faithful may rely upon the finding in the first action to prevent Gotschall from relitigating the issue. See Restatement (Second) of Judgments §28(1). So, under either approach, the court grants summary judgment for Faithful.

Final answer: B

This question illustrates several important points about collateral estoppel. First, note that this is a case of non-mutual estoppel. Carmichael was not a party to the earlier action; she seeks to rely upon the findings in that action to prevent Faithful from relitigating them here. Since the federal courts permit non-mutual estoppel, we need to consider whether the requirements for applying it are met. D takes us back to basics. It suggests that the court will bar Faithful from relitigating the representation claim, even though it won on that issue in the previous action, because the finding wasn’t necessary to support the judgment. But that isn’t right. Collateral estoppel bars relitigation of issues that were actually litigated and decided in the prior action, regardless of their effect on the outcome. If the losing party litigates an issue and loses, she shouldn’t get another chance just because the winning party didn’t need the favorable ruling to win the case. So D fails. B asserts that Carmichael hasn’t litigated the representation issue, so she gets to try it over again. That’s true, but irrelevant. The question is whether Faithful has litigated the issue before. It has, and lost. C states that Faithful hasn’t litigated the refund provision issue against Carmichael, so it should be allowed to raise it again. Again, that’s true, but beside the point. Faithful has litigated the refund issue once, and lost. Even though it hasn’t litigated it against Carmichael, it has litigated it before, and lost. And that means that it cannot relitigate it unless the court concludes that application of estoppel would be unfair. A is the best choice. Both issues were litigated and decided in the Gotschall action. Although Carmichael herself did not participate in that action, Faithful did, and lost on these issues. Thus, the court would likely hold that Faithful is collaterally estopped from relitigating them in Carmichael’s action.

Final answer: A
